articleOfWeek.title: Ventilator-circuit configurations for noninvasive ventilation in infants with acute respiratory failure: a randomized crossover trial.
articleOfWeek.abstract: Patient-ventilator synchrony may differ across ventilator and circuit configurations during noninvasive ventilation (NIV) in infants. We compared an intentional-leak single-limb turbine configuration (SLC-turbine), a dual-limb turbine configuration with an active expiratory valve (DLC-turbine), and a dual-limb compressed-gas pediatric ICU configuration (DLC-PICU) in infants receiving NIV for acute respiratory failure METHODS: In this single-center randomized crossover physiological study, infants underwent three 30-minute NIV phases in randomized order with unchanged pressure support, PEEP, and FiO₂. Esophageal pressure was used to assess the asynchrony index (AI), individual asynchronies, and inspiratory effort. Primary and secondary endpoints were AI differences between DLC-PICU and SLC-turbine and between DLC-PICU and DLC-turbine, respectively RESULTS: Twenty infants entered stabilization, 13 were randomized, and 12 completed the protocol (age 10 [7-21] months; SpO₂/FiO₂ 185 [160-220]). AI differed across configurations: 8.6% [6.7-16.5] with SLC-turbine, 25.4% [16.3-35.0] with DLC-turbine, and 45.7% [30.5-63.8] with DLC-PICU (p=0.0023). AI was higher with DLC-PICU than with SLC-turbine (Hodges-Lehmann difference +32.0%, 95% CI +13.9 to +50.1; p=0.0015) and DLC-turbine (+18.4%, 95% CI +5.9 to +36.3; p=0.021). Auto-triggering showed the clearest configuration-dependent difference and was more frequent with DLC-PICU than with SLC-turbine (7.5 [0.6-11.4] vs 0 [0-2.5] events/min; difference +5.30 events/min; p=0.0039), without a significant difference between DLC-PICU and DLC-turbine. Ineffective efforts, double triggering, and premature cycling did not differ across configurations. All NIV configurations reduced inspiratory effort versus unassisted spontaneous breathing, with no significant differences among NIV configurations CONCLUSIONS: AI was lower with SLC-turbine and DLC-turbine than with DLC-PICU and lowest with SLC-turbine. Auto-triggering showed the clearest configuration-dependent difference. All configurations reduced inspiratory effort versus unassisted spontaneous breathing, without significant between-configuration differences. Because ventilator platform, circuit and expiratory architecture, and device-specific control functions differed, effects of individual components cannot be determined. These findings are specific to the ventilators and configurations evaluated. Further studies should determine whether these physiological differences translate into improved NIV tolerance or short- and long-term clinical outcomes TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04017780. Registered on 12 July 2019.

articles.title: How I Do It: An Intensivist's guide to RV Failure and Right Ventricular Assist Devices.
authors: Cardiology/CV Surgery Section, Pulmonary Vascular Disease and Cardiovascular Network.
articles.abstract: Right ventricular failure (RVF) is a high-mortality form of cardiogenic shock frequently encountered in critical illness and is often underrecognized due to its heterogeneous presentation. This article presents a physiology-driven, stepwise approach to the diagnosis and management of acute RVF using a longitudinal case in the intensive care unit. We highlight practical bedside tools for recognition, including point-of-care ultrasound and invasive hemodynamics, and review targeted strategies for preload optimization, afterload reduction, and contractility support. Special emphasis is placed on airway management, vasoactive medications, and timely escalation to mechanical circulatory support (MCS) in appropriately selected patients. This bedside "How I Do It" guide is written for intensivists and pulmonary/critical care clinicians and translates advanced hemodynamic and device concepts into practical decision points for acute care management.

articles.title: Positive pressure ventilation in newborns at birth: a systematic review of recipient characteristics and temporal trends.
articles.abstract: To synthesise evidence on temporal trends, recipient characteristics and variation in the use of positive pressure ventilation (PPV) at birth. This systematic review was registered (CRD42024487025) and followed a condition-context-population framework. Five electronic databases and grey literature were searched to 25 June 2026. Risk of bias was assessed using the JBI checklist, and reporting followed PRISMA 2020. Forty-two studies from 34 countries (27 from high-income countries), reporting 269 to 10,696,831 livebirths per study (1984-2024), were included. Heterogeneity in whether continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) was distinguished from PPV, interface definitions and eligibility criteria precluded meta-analysis. Fifteen studies included only preterm infants and 19 excluded congenital anomalies. Nine population-based and large multicentre studies that excluded CPAP and included all age groups reported PPV incidence ranging from 3.0% to 8.0%. Rates were much higher among very and extremely preterm infants. Temporal trends suggested increasing PPV incidence overall and via facemask, whereas tracheal-tube PPV was stable or declining. Lower PPV incidence was reported in low-resource and lower-level birthing centres. Few studies reported indications for or timing of PPV initiation, and reported data items were inconsistent. PPV remains common in neonatal resuscitation, with higher use at lower gestational ages and higher-level birthing services. Limited and heterogeneous reporting of indications and PPV timelines constrains interpretation and comparison. Standardised, neonatal Utstein-aligned reporting, including PPV indications and time intervals and separate reporting of airway interfaces and CPAP, is needed. Further population-based studies, particularly in low-and middle-income countries, are warranted.

Ultrasound-Guided Suprascapular Nerve Block Versus Intravenous Fentanyl for Analgesia in Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department With Traumatic Scapular Fractures.
articles.abstract: To compare the analgesic efficacy and safety of ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block with intravenous fentanyl in patients with traumatic scapular fractures. We conducted an open-label randomized controlled pilot trial in the emergency department (ED) of a Level I trauma center in North India. Adults with traumatic scapular fractures and Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale scores of 7 and higher, were randomly assigned to ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block or intravenous fentanyl (1 μg/kg). Pain scores were assessed at baseline and 30, 60, 120, 240, and 360 minutes. Secondary outcomes included rescue analgesia and adverse events. Sixty patients were randomly assigned to the 2 groups. Median baseline pain score was 10 in both groups. Pain scores were consistently lower with suprascapular nerve block, with median scores of 3 (interquartile [IQR] 2 to 5) versus 7 (IQR 6 to 8) at 30 minutes. Between-group differences were 4 (95% confidence interval [CI], 3 to 4) at 30 and 60 minutes, 2 (95% CI, 2 to 2) at 120 and 240 minutes, and 1 (95% CI, 1 to 2) at 360 minutes. Rescue analgesia was less frequent with suprascapular nerve block (13% versus 79%; risk difference, -66% [95% CI, 47.5 to 85.2]). Drowsiness was more common with fentanyl (12 versus 2 participants); hypotension occurred in 1 fentanyl recipient and paresthesia in 1 suprascapular nerve block recipient. In this pilot randomized trial, ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block provided greater and sustained pain relief, reduced rescue analgesia, and fewer systemic adverse effects than intravenous fentanyl in adults with traumatic scapular fractures. Larger multicenter trials are needed to confirm these findings and evaluate cumulative opioid use and longer-term outcomes.

articles.title: MPLA preconditioning protects against lethal radiation-combined burn injury with attenuation of KC/CXCL1-associated vascular leakage in mice.
articles.abstract: Radiation-combined burn injury (RCB), defined as concurrent irradiation and burn injury, is expected to be common in radiological or nuclear mass-casualty events and can be highly lethal. The mechanisms underlying the irradiation-burn interaction remain poorly understood, particularly whether it amplifies capillary leak and inflammatory mediator responses to drive early lethality. We examined whether repeated low-dose monophosphoryl lipid A (MPLA) preconditioning modulates this response and whether KC/CXCL1 contributes to vascular leakage. Male C57BL/6J mice underwent 6 Gy whole-body irradiation followed 1 h later by a 20% total body surface area full-thickness burn. MPLA (10 µg/mouse) or vehicle was administered intraperitoneally on days -4 and -3. We assessed 30-day survival, hemoconcentration, intravascular FITC-albumin retention, intestinal barrier endpoints, and cytokine/chemokine responses. A separate exploratory experiment evaluated pre-irradiation anti-KC/CXCL1 antibody treatment. Neither injury alone was lethal, whereas vehicle-treated RCB mice had 90% mortality (9 of 10 mice). Seven of these deaths occurred at 24-48 h after RCB. MPLA preconditioning increased 30-day survival from 10% to 80% (p = 0.0003) and eliminated deaths within 48 h. RCB induced hemoconcentration and tended to reduce FITC-albumin retention. Compared with vehicle-treated RCB mice, MPLA-preconditioned RCB mice had less hemoconcentration, significantly higher FITC-albumin retention, and lower mesenteric lymph node bacterial burden. MPLA preconditioning suppressed KC/CXCL1, which showed the largest absolute increase among measured cytokines/chemokines at 6 h. Anti-KC/CXCL1 antibody treatment significantly increased FITC-albumin retention at 6 h (p = 0.038). MPLA preconditioning improved survival after RCB. It may attenuate early inflammatory and vascular abnormalities. Exploratory antibody-treatment findings suggest a possible contribution of KC/CXCL1 to early vascular albumin leakage, warranting further validation.

Trends in United States Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Incidence and Mortality in a Nationally Representative Sample, 2009-2022.
articles.abstract: National estimates of pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) incidence in the United States rely on a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative datasets offer a nationally representative alternative. We estimated nationally representative pediatric IHCA incidence and mortality trends from 2009 through 2022. Serial cross-sectional analysis of five triennial editions of the Kids' Inpatient Database (2009-2022), identifying IHCA in children <18 years by ICD-9 (99.60, 99.63) and ICD-10 (5A12012) cardiopulmonary resuscitation procedure codes. Two hospitals with implausible CPR rates were excluded. Survey-weighted incidence per 1,000 hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality among resuscitated children were estimated overall and by neonatal status, complex chronic condition (CCC) status, ZIP-code income quartile, and US Census region. Trends were tested with survey-weighted quasi-Poisson regression across the full period and, as exploratory analyses, within the ICD-10 era (2016-2022). Observed IHCA incidence was 1.11/1,000 in 2009 and 1.22/1,000 in 2012, decreased to 1.11/1,000 at the ICD-10 transition and increased to 1.35/1,000 by 2022. IHCA incidence in children hospitalized with a CCC rose from 3.26 to 6.60/1,000 (6.2%/year, p<0.001), while incidence without CCC remained low. Incidence varied by socioeconomic status (lowest vs highest income quartile 1.78 vs 1.04/1,000 in 2022). In-hospital mortality ranged from 34.1% (2012) to 40.4% (2019), whereas IHCA deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased 1.7%/year (p<0.001), concentrated among children with a CCC. The incidence of pediatric IHCA increased among hospitalizations involving children with CCC and was higher among children who live in lower income areas. In-hospital mortality after CPR was largely stable, whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased among children with CCC. A single hospital's coding practices can materially distort national administrative estimates. What is already known Pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest affects approximately 15,200 children annually in the United States, with this national estimate derived primarily from a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative databases offer nationally representative coverage but rely on procedure codes that are susceptible to misclassification. What this study adds In this nationally representative administrative database sample spanning 2009-2022, this study demonstrated that: 1) the incidence of IHCA among children with complex chronic conditions (CCC) rose steadily and accounted for the substantial majority of events, 2) the overall IHCA incidence was higher among children who live in lower income areas with the gradient worsening over the period evaluated, and 3) in-hospital mortality after CPR increased only slightly (34-40%), whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased more, driven mainly by rising incidence among children with CCC, and 4) CPR coding at a single hospital can substantially distort national administrative estimates.

Carboxypeptidase B1: A novel, targetable contributor to thromboembolic complications in severe acute pancreatitis?
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) is associated with increased thrombotic risk. Systemic release of pancreatic proteases in SAP may alter susceptibility to endogenous fibrinolysis, but this remains unexplored. Pancreatic carboxypeptidase B1 (CPB1) is a protease activated by trypsin that shares cleavage specificity with thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor, which cleaves C-terminal lysine residues off fibrin, impairing co-localization of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and plasminogen and rendering clots resistant to fibrinolysis. We hypothesized that circulating CPB1 would be elevated in SAP patients and contribute to fibrinolytic resistance. Plasma and clinical data were prospectively collected from SAP patients (n=15), matched critically ill controls without pancreatitis (n=13), and healthy controls (n=4) with IRB approval and informed consent. CPB1 levels were measured through ELISA. Clot lysis assays assessed fibrinolysis in response to tPA. Healthy control plasma was tested with and without porcine pancreas CPB1 to assess the effect of CPB1 on fibrinolysis. Transition midpoints (TM's) were defined as the time to 50% clot lysis. Clinical data were analyzed using Mann-Whitney U and Fisher exact tests. Assay results were analyzed using Kruskall-Wallis test. Significance was set at P<0.05. Demographics were similar between groups. SAP patients had markedly elevated CPB1 levels (154.0 [58.4-388.0] ng/mL) compared with sick (7.0 [4.1-15.6] ng/mL, P<0.0001) and healthy controls (4.0 [2.1-4.4], P<0.001). Healthy control plasma supplemented with porcine pancreas CPB1 demonstrated complete disruption of fibrinolysis compared with healthy plasma without CPB1. SAP patients had the highest resistance to tPA-induced fibrinolysis, with significantly higher baseline TMs than critically ill controls (42.0 [21.7-126.6] vs. 22.8 [18.3-33.7], P=0.04). Patients with SAP have uniquely elevated circulating levels of CPB1, which may contribute to thromboembolism in SAP through fibrinolytic resistance. Further investigation into targeted CPB1 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy in SAP is warranted to potentially reduce development of organ failure and mortality. N/A (Basic Science).

Comparative Effectiveness of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists versus DPP-4 and SGLT2 Inhibitors in Patients with Bronchiectasis and Type 2 Diabetes.
articles.abstract: Bronchiectasis is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with limited disease-modifying therapies. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, but their impact on bronchiectasis outcomes remains unknown. Is GLP-1RA use, compared with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i) or sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) use, associated with better clinical outcomes in patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes (T2D)? Using the TriNetX global federated research network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes who initiated GLP-1RA therapy between June 1, 2022, and May 30, 2025. We compared clinical outcomes, including all-cause mortality, bronchiectasis exacerbation, acute respiratory failure, and lower respiratory tract infections, with patients receiving DPP-4i) or SGLT2i using propensity score matching to balance baseline characteristics. After propensity score matching, 1,029 patients per group were included in the GLP-1RA versus DPP-4i cohort, and 2,255 patients per group in the GLP-1RA versus SGLT2i cohort. Compared with DPP-4i, GLP-1RA use was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 0.43; 95% CI, 0.33-0.56) and reduced risks of acute respiratory failure (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.36-0.58) and lower respiratory tract infection (HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.46-0.65). Similar benefits were observed compared with SGLT2i for all-cause mortality (HR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.40-0.60), acute respiratory failure (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.39-0.55), and lower respiratory tract infection (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.68-0.86). Stratified analyses demonstrated consistent mortality benefits across demographic and clinical subgroups, with particularly pronounced effects in obese patients but there was no statistically significant reduction in bronchiectasis exacerbations. Among patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes, GLP-1RA therapy was associated with significantly lower mortality and reduced respiratory complications compared with DPP-4i or SGLT2i. These findings suggest potential disease-modifying benefits of GLP-1RAs in bronchiectasis beyond glycemic control.

articles.title: The Burden of Chronic Cough in Patients With Interstitial Lung Disease: a US Survey-Based Analysis of Its Effects on Daily Life and Emotional and Social Well-Being.
articles.abstract: Chronic cough (≥8 weeks) is highly prevalent among patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and non-IPF interstitial lung disease (ILD) and imposes significant physical, social, and psychological burden. Research characterizing the burden of chronic cough in patients with IPF and non-IPF ILD from the patient perspective is limited. What is the multidimensional burden of chronic cough in patients living with IPF or non-IPF ILD? An online cross-sectional survey was distributed to adults from June to July 2025 via the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation's US Community Registry. Eligibility required a self-reported diagnosis of IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough. Multiple-choice and open-text questions spanned six domains: demographics, disease history, cough characteristics, daily life impact, social/emotional and long-term impact, and healthcare experience. A total of 197 participants completed the survey: 75.63% reported a diagnosis of IPF, 21.32% reported non-IPF ILD, and 3.05% were awaiting further ILD diagnosis. Participants reported cough-related interference with daily activities (76.15%) and sleep disruption (79.69%) within the preceding week. Emotional burden was frequently reported: 95.94% of participants had cough-induced worry, 75.13% had depression, sadness, or low mood, and 67.01% reported avoiding social situations because of cough. Additionally, 60.91% of participants reported that chronic cough affected their platonic relationships, and 55.33% reported impact on their ability or desire to maintain physical or intimate relationships. To treat cough, participants reported using an average of 2.7 therapeutic classes historically and 2.0 classes currently, with many reporting limited or no relief. Findings from this US survey of patients with IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough indicate that, among respondents, chronic cough burden manifests physically, psychologically, and psychosocially. Reports of limited relief from available therapies suggest an unmet need in managing chronic cough in this patient population. Not applicable.
